about.title: Printing and Schools: Copying at Scale
about.length_note: About 40 minutes. The class has five topics, and each is taught in short steps with a check question. The historians' debate over whether print fixed texts is kept short in the lesson and set out in full in other_side, so the pace stays steady.

say.text: Welcome to class five. Today's question is simple. How did knowledge get cheaper to copy, and how did more people get to learn it?

show.text: Printing and Schools: Copying at Scale

say.text: Remember the ratchet from class one? A ratchet clicks forward and does not slip back. Culture works like that when each generation keeps what the last one learned.
A ratchet only holds if knowledge can be copied. Copying is the click. Today we follow how copying got faster, cheaper and wider, in five steps.

show.text: 1. Hand copying | 2. Printing in Asia and Europe | 3. The printing house | 4. Schools and literacy | 5. Standard texts, good and bad

say.text: Step one. Before printing in Europe, one scribe copied one book at a time. One pen, one page, one book.

show.text: One scribe, one book at a time

say.text: People who copy by hand slip. They skip a line, misspell a word, or misread one. The next scribe may then copy that slip as if it were right.
Quick check on that idea.

show.text: Check: a slip in the source

ask.q: A scribe copies a book that already has a slip in it. What may happen to the slip?
ask.right: It can be copied into the new book too.
wrong: It turns into a new chapter.
ask.why: The scribe works from the copy in front of them, so a slip in the source can travel on.

say.text: To be fair, scribes also noticed and fixed mistakes. Errors did not simply pile up forever. Hand copying was careful work. It was just slow and costly.

show.text: Hand copying: slow, one book at a time, slips can travel | But: scribes also spotted and corrected errors

say.text: How slow? Before printing, Europe's manuscript books could be counted in thousands. By 1500, after about fifty years of printing, there were more than nine million.

show.text: More than 9,000,000 books in Europe by 1500

say.text: Prices fell too. One study finds that book production rose after the mid-1400s probably because books got cheaper and more people could read.
Let's check the size of that change.

show.text: Thousands before printing; over 9 million by 1500

ask.q: How did the number of books in Europe change between the time before printing and 1500?
ask.right: From thousands to more than nine million.
wrong: From millions to slightly more millions.
It fell, because books became rare.
ask.why: Britannica says manuscript books were counted in thousands before printing, and there were more than 9,000,000 books by 1500.

say.text: Step two. Printing began in East Asia. In woodblock printing, a whole page is carved into a block of wood, inked and pressed onto paper. One block makes many copies.
The oldest dated printed book we know is the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist text from China. Its date is 11 May 868.

show.text: the earliest, dated, printed book in the world

say.text: It was found by accident in a hidden cave at Dunhuang, in northwest China, along with tens of thousands of other scrolls. Today it is kept at the British Library.

show.text: A long paper scroll. At its start, a carved black-ink picture of the Buddha teaching. It lay in a sealed cave near Dunhuang until about 1900.

say.text: Time to check that.

ask.q: What is the Diamond Sutra known for?
ask.right: It is the oldest dated printed book we know, from 868.
wrong: It was the first book ever written.
It was the first book printed with metal type.
It was the first book printed in Europe.
ask.why: Its date of 11 May 868 makes it the earliest dated printed book known, and it was made in China.

say.text: Next idea: movable type. Instead of carving a whole page, you make separate pieces, one for each character, and rearrange them for every page. Then you reuse the pieces.
Around 1041, in Song China, an artisan named Bi Sheng made movable type from clay pieces. They could be arranged to print one page, then rearranged for another.
Movable type did not take over in China. Chinese writing uses thousands of different characters, so printers needed a huge set of pieces. Woodblock stayed popular for East Asian text.
Check that reason.

ask.q: Why did woodblock printing often stay more popular than movable type for Chinese text?
ask.right: Chinese needs thousands of different characters, so a huge set of pieces was required.
wrong: Movable type was against the law.
Ink had not been invented yet.
ask.why: Movable type needs reusable pieces for each character, and Chinese has thousands of them.

say.text: Korea took movable type further. By the 13th century Korean printers had movable metal type. The oldest surviving book printed with metal type is the Jikji, from Korea in 1377.
So when Johannes Gutenberg worked in Mainz, Germany, in the 1450s, he did not invent printing with movable type. He built on earlier ideas.
What he did was combine parts into one working system. He used a goldsmith's skill to make a casting metal, molds for even letters, and a modified screw press.

show.text: Casting metal for type | Molds for even letters | A modified screw press

say.text: Now a number check. The Diamond Sutra is from 868. Gutenberg's press in Europe is from the 1450s.

ask.q: About how many years came between the 868 Diamond Sutra and Gutenberg's press in the 1450s?
ask.why: 1450 minus 868 is 582, so printing existed in Asia roughly six centuries before Gutenberg.

say.text: Printing spread, but not everywhere at once. It reached England in 1476. In 1500 England still had only five printers, all in London and all foreigners.
Step three. Step inside a printing house. Plantin's, in Antwerp, is a museum today, and the 16th-century workshop is almost completely intact.
In 1575 it had 56 men. There were 32 printers, 20 compositors, three proofreaders and one unskilled labourer. The museum says it was the largest business of its kind in the world then.
A compositor is the person who sets the type. They placed lead letters into a composing stick to make a line. A compositor could usually prepare one forme a day, a frame of type ready for the press.

show.text: A worker at a wooden stand of type cases, picking small lead letters into a hand-held stick to build a line of text.

say.text: Correctors were scholars who spoke several languages. They read the proofs between typesetting and printing, helped by a reader who read aloud.
Let's check the roles.

show.text: Check: roles in the printing house

ask.q: In Plantin's printing house, what did a corrector do?
ask.right: Read the proofs and checked for mistakes between typesetting and printing.
wrong: Sold the finished books in the shop.
ask.why: Correctors sat by the window and carefully read the proofs made after typesetting and before the actual printing.

say.text: The shop was busy. Day after day, 1,250 sheets rolled off the presses, and more than 50 workers kept everything running.
A printing house was also a trade network. Papermakers, bookbinders, engravers and booksellers outside the shop all took part. Plantin printed bibles, humanist works and scientific books.

show.text: Papermakers | Bookbinders | Engravers | Booksellers | Editors, typesetters, printers, proofreaders

say.text: Even here, printed copies could differ. Corrections were made while pressmen kept printing, so some books ended up with more than one text variant.
Step four. A school is a system for handing learning to many people on a regular plan. Printing made books cheaper. Schools made readers.
Universities grew out of church schools. Bologna, founded in 1088, is called the mother of European universities. Its exact founding date is uncertain.

Universities needed many copies of the same textbooks, long before printing. Their answer was the pecia system. An approved master copy was split into sections of about four leaves and rented out to be copied.

show.text: Pecia: a master copy rented out in pieces

say.text: Committees of teachers checked the master copies and posted lists of approved texts. Bologna had about 119 legal texts on its list in the early 1300s. That is an early standard text.

show.text: About 119 approved legal texts, Bologna, early 1300s

say.text: Check what pecia means.

ask.right: A way of renting out sections of an approved master copy so many copies could be made.
ask.why: A master copy, or exemplar, was divided into sections and rented to students or scribes to copy.

say.text: Reading is the key that opens written knowledge. Early demand for books came mostly from monasteries. Later it came from universities and ordinary readers.

show.text: Literacy: the key to written knowledge

say.text: Schooling for nearly everyone came much later. Prussia issued a school regulation in 1763, and by 1816 it led the world in primary schooling.
By 1816 about 58 in every 100 children aged 6 to 14 were enrolled, on average. By 1849 it was about 80. In 1871 adult literacy averaged 84 percent.
Prussia was among the first places with tax-funded, generally compulsory primary schooling. France and Britain did not manage it until the 1880s.
Now the whole world. In 1820 only about one adult in ten could read. Today about 87 in every 100 can.

show.text: Share of the world's adults who can read and write

say.text: Check that number.

ask.q: Around 1820, about what share of the world's adults could read and write?
ask.why: Our World in Data estimates that only about every tenth adult was literate in 1820, compared with about 87% today.

say.text: Step five. A standard text is one version that many people share. Everyone can read, quote and check the same words.

Historian Elizabeth Eisenstein argued that print gave writing a fixity. People could compare texts, correct them, and share a common standard. That suits a ratchet. Many people can build on, check and fix the same text.
But a press copies anything. In the 1500s Netherlands, printed media was a much-feared weapon, and about 8 percent of Plantin's output was ordered by political authorities.

show.text: Good: shared, checkable texts | Bad: copies mistakes and persuasion too

say.text: Early printing was a restless, competitive free-for-all. It only began to be regulated and controlled after about 1550.
Schools could shape loyalty too. One study says Prussia used mass schooling to build a more unified citizenry and strengthen the state.
Check both sides.

ask.right: Printing and schools spread knowledge, and they can also spread mistakes or shape what people believe.
wrong: Printing only ever spread the truth.
Schools never affect what people believe.
ask.why: The same tools that copy knowledge can copy errors and persuasion, and states have used schools to build loyalty.

say.text: Historians still argue about this. Eisenstein calls print an agent of change, not the only one. Adrian Johns says fixity and standardization were built by people over time and were not built into print.

show.text: Eisenstein: print gave fixity and standard texts | Johns: fixity was achieved by people, not automatic

say.text: Let's put the story in order on the timeline.

show.text: 868 Diamond Sutra printed, China | about 1041 Bi Sheng's clay type | 1088 Bologna university | 1377 Jikji, metal type, Korea | 1450s Gutenberg, Mainz | 1476 printing reaches England | 1500 over 9 million books in Europe | 1575 Plantin's house: 56 men | 1763 Prussian school regulation | 1816 Prussia: 58% of children enrolled | 1880s compulsory schooling in France and Britain

say.text: Use the timeline to answer this one.

ask.q: Which came first: the Korean Jikji, or Gutenberg's press in Europe?
wrong: They came in the same year.
ask.why: The Jikji was printed in 1377. Gutenberg worked in the 1450s, so the Korean book came about 78 years earlier.

say.text: Let's gather it up. Copying by hand was slow and slips could travel. Printing made copies faster and cheaper. Schools and literacy made more readers. Standard texts let people share and check the same words.

show.text: Hand copying: slow, slips can travel | Printing: faster, cheaper copies | Schools: more readers | Standard texts: shared and checkable | Both good and bad uses

say.text: One last check, back to the ratchet.

ask.q: How does cheaper, wider copying help the ratchet?
ask.right: Knowledge reaches more people in a more checkable form, so fewer gains slip back.
wrong: It makes people invent new things automatically.
It stops anyone from ever making a mistake.
It means nobody needs to learn to read.
ask.why: Cheaper books and more readers mean more people hold the same knowledge and can check it, so it is less likely to be lost.

notes.topic: How knowledge gets lost, the other side of the ratchet
History-of-everything timeline: 868 to the 1880s on this class's timeline beat
Source choice: estimates of early book numbers differ between sources. This class uses Britannica's figure of more than 9 million books by 1500.
Source choice: sources describe Prussia's 1763 regulation differently, as obligatory for rural Protestants or as a general invitation to attend school. The lesson says only 'school regulation'.

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: While Bi Sheng was making clay movable type in Song China, the University of Bologna, the 'mother of European universities', was forming. Its exact founding date is uncertain.
European universities multiplied. Oxford is dated 1167, Cambridge 1209, Paris 1215 and Padua 1222. In Korea, printers developed movable metal type by the 13th century.
Korea printed the Jikji with metal type. In Europe, universities were still supplied by hand copying, since they were founded before the printing press.
Gutenberg worked in Mainz, and printing reached England in 1476. By 1500 Europe had more than 9 million books.
Prussia built an early system of primary schooling. Around 1820 only about one adult in ten in the world could read.
France and Britain finally enacted compulsory schooling, about a century after Prussia's first steps.

other_side.claim: Print gave texts fixity and a shared standard, which made knowledge more reliable and cumulative.
other_side.other_view: Elizabeth Eisenstein argued that print let people compare and correct texts and gave a common standard. Adrian Johns replied that fixity and standardization were not built into print. Early modern people had to achieve them through social effort, and early printed copies varied. Eisenstein herself called print an agent of change, not the only agent. Plantin's own shop produced books with variant texts.
Woodblock printing and movable type, including Korean metal type, came earlier in East Asia. Gutenberg combined and improved existing methods. How printing knowledge reached Europe is uncertain.

other_side.claim: Hand copying was hopeless, because errors piled up with each copy.
other_side.other_view: Slips did happen and could be copied on. But scribes also noticed and corrected errors, so errors did not simply pile up with each copy. Monasteries also had rules to limit corruption.

other_side.claim: Mass schooling was simply a gift of knowledge to everyone.
other_side.other_view: Schooling brought reading and basic skills. But one study says Prussia also used mass schooling to build a unified citizenry and strengthen state power. The Prussian schools also stressed duty and discipline.
